title: Opening Range Breakout
teaches: The opening range breakout as we trade it: an entry timer on 30-minute bars for a daily setup already on the focus list (a Kicker, an earnings gap, a base breakout) in a leader above its 50-day and 200-day; the range is the first 30-minute candle, 9:30 to 10:00 ET; the buy is the trade a cent through its high after 10:00 at market, never more than 4% past it; the stop sits a few cents under the day's low at the fill; a third comes off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail; on a Kicker the stop is capped at 3.5%; a loss at the stop is the plan working.

facts.quote: In this book I define the Opening Range as the first 30 minutes of the trading day.
facts.claim: Bysshe defines the opening range as the first 30 minutes of the day.

facts.quote: the 30-minute OR is defined as the stock's high and low for the day at 10:00 AM. The OR is not the opening price.
facts.claim: Bysshe: the 30-minute range is the day's high and low at 10:00, not the opening print.

facts.quote: If the OR is sloppy, that is, if there isn't any well-defined support or resistance, don't waste your time watching it.
facts.claim: Bysshe skips a sloppy range with no well-defined high or low.

facts.quote: The daily trend should be positive. Both the 20-day and the 50-day moving averages are positively sloped and the stock is trading above the 20-day moving average.
facts.claim: Bysshe wants a positive daily trend: rising 20 and 50-day averages, price above the 20-day.

facts.quote: A bullish bias pattern in the OR may give you a hint, but your best clue is volume.
facts.claim: Bysshe: the best clue in the opening range is volume.

facts.quote: a period of time equal to half the time period of the OR.
facts.claim: Bysshe's clean-break rule of thumb: after the break, price holds above the range for a period equal to half the range's own length, which is 15 minutes on a 30-minute range.

facts.quote: your maximum risk point for an OR breakout is the low of the OR.
facts.claim: Bysshe's widest stop on a range break is the range low.

facts.quote: If I can't find a good stop or risk point then I generally pass on the trade.
facts.claim: Bysshe passes when no good stop can be found.

facts.quote: First identify a list of candidates based on your swing trade criteria, and then use the OR to time your entry.
facts.claim: Bysshe: pick the swing candidates first, then use the opening range to time the entry.

facts.quote: The result is you buy a stock that has already moved too far from your optimal entry point.
facts.claim: Bysshe on chasing a strong open: you buy too far from the right entry.

facts.quote: Enter on the opening range highs.
facts.claim: Kullamagi enters a breakout at the opening range high.

facts.quote: The opening range highs can be the highs of the first 1-minute candle, the 5-minute candle or the 60-minute candle (on the 60-minute timeframe the first candle is always only 30 minutes, 9.30-10 AM).
facts.claim: Kullamagi: on a 60-minute chart the first candle is only 30 minutes, 9:30 to 10:00.

facts.quote: Stop is always lows of the day and stop should not be wider than the ATR or ADR of the stock
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the stop is the low of the day, no wider than the stock's ATR or ADR.

facts.quote: Many times the best ones have traded their average daily volume in the first 15-30 minutes after the open.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the best gap plays trade their average daily volume in the first 15 to 30 minutes.

facts.quote: You should sell 1/3 to 1/2 of the position after 3-5 days, and then move the stop to break even.
facts.claim: Kullamagi sells a third to a half after 3 to 5 days, then moves the stop to breakeven.

facts.quote: You don’t even have to use any intraday chart, just look at the daily chart and enter when the stock is starting to break out.
facts.claim: Kullamagi: the setup is on the daily chart; the intraday chart only times the entry.

facts.quote: The 30-minute opening range is the high and low of the first 30 minute candle of the day. An opening range breakout is the first time price trades above that high.
facts.claim: Trade-Ideas: the 30-minute range is the first 30-minute candle's high and low; the breakout is the first trade above that high.

facts.quote: The morning range is defined by the high and low made in the first 45-120 minutes. Different time parameters can be used, but the most popular one is the first hour's range.
facts.claim: Raschke's morning range is longer, 45 to 120 minutes; windows differ by trader.

facts.quote: The good news is that breakout strategies have a high win/loss ratio. The bad news is that whipsaws can be brutal!
facts.claim: Raschke: breakout strategies win often, and the whipsaws are brutal.

facts.quote: An opening range breakout (ORB) is a trade taken at a predetermined amount above or below the opening range.
facts.claim: Crabel's definition: a trade taken a set amount beyond the opening range.

facts.quote: My hypothesis is that inside days precede trend day activity and, consequently, successful opening range breakouts.
facts.claim: Crabel: inside days precede trend days and successful opening range breakouts.

facts.quote: This makes the first pullback after the breakout move a nice high-probability entry once you start to see resumed buying.
facts.claim: Steenbarger likes the first pullback after a valid break, once buying resumes.

facts.quote: Crabel took profits quite quickly, usually at the close of the first trading day or on the first profitable close.
facts.claim: StockCharts: Crabel took profits at the first day's close or the first profitable close.

The ORB entry, a cent over the first 30-minute high, fills at 11.21: 3.7% to the same stop, the confirmation.
The cap: 3.5% under 11.21 is 10.82, the Kicker low itself. At the close: the first entry 2.3R, the ORB 1.0R.

The clock: section 9 of the dossier grades an early trigger (by about 10:30) higher, resting on Zarattini's 5-minute result; the scan's one window found later triggers did better (34.5% to 3R after 10:30 against 22.5% by 10:30). q31 keys only what is settled (D-143: the trigger stays valid all session) and the card's 'later triggers grade lower' as the card's cue; the number is never keyed.

The trigger: every outside source acts on the trade through (Crabel's and Raschke's stop orders, Trade-Ideas, Kullamagi); only the app's scanner waits for a 5-minute close. The unit keys the trade through (c02, t01) and never mentions the scanner to a member.

The stop: Crabel, Raschke and Bysshe's maximum use the opposite side of the range; Kullamagi and the owner use the low of the day. On a first break after 10:00 the two usually agree. The unit keys the house stop (A3, F62): a few cents under the day's low at the fill. Bysshe's 'maximum risk point' (b07) supports it and is never keyed as ours.

The hold: Crabel's tests and Zarattini exit the same day; Raschke overnight; Kullamagi sells a third to a half after 3 to 5 days. The card is a swing trade (C35) with the house trims; q36 and q62 teach the others' exits as theirs, never ours.

The exit on a reversal: Bysshe calls a big-volume reversal at the top of the range a failed breakout; A4 keeps the stop as the only exit. q40 keys the card's settled line (a warning, not a second exit rule) with the APA loss as the planned loss.

Walk-through fills: the scan filled at the range high plus a cent (FFIV 418.46, SNX 274.04) or at the bar's open when it gapped over, and stopped 5 cents under the day's low at the fill; a live market order fills a little differently. JBI's numbers (w3) are the card's own evidence row from the owner's 2026-11-02 ruling and the repo's 30-minute bars.

The unit id SET.32 is the plan's (UNITS-method.md: 'ORB (Opening Range Break)', M11.L1); its row describes 'the aggressive range-break timer on the open' and names the 30-Minute Pivot as a sibling; the dossier's D-002 note separates the two (ORB = the first trade through the first half-hour's high; the pivot = the turn candle at support), which this unit follows.

questions.q: What is the opening range on our ORB?
choices: The 9:30 to 10:00 high and low
The first 5-minute bar's range
The 9:30 opening print alone
The 9:30 to 10:30 high and low
questions.why: The 9:30 to 10:00 high and low, the first 30-minute candle. Trade-Ideas defines the 30-minute range as the high and low of the first 30-minute candle. Bysshe says it is the day's high and low at 10:00, not the opening price. Other windows are other traders' choices, not ours.
questions.lesson_line: The range is the first half hour. Mark its high and low at 10:00.

wrong.The first 5-minute bar's range: That is the opening drive's bar, a different timer: a drive is bought over the first 5-minute bar's high by about 9:40. Our range is the full 30 minutes.
wrong.The 9:30 opening print alone: Bysshe: the OR is not the opening price. It is a high and a low.
wrong.The 9:30 to 10:30 high and low: Raschke's morning range runs 45 to 120 minutes, and windows differ by trader. Ours ends at 10:00.

questions.simple: Our range is the high and low of the first half hour, from 9:30 to 10:00.

deeper.counter: Windows differ across traders. Raschke defines a morning range of 45 to 120 minutes, most popularly the first hour. Kullamagi allows the first 1-minute, 5-minute or 60-minute candle. Bysshe and Trade-Ideas use the first 30 minutes, as we do. The 30-minute window is our house default, so the range we mark is 9:30 to 10:00.

reasons: rests on the house 30-minute window (D-031 pending; 30 minutes kept as the default in every option)

questions.q: The ORB trigger is a trade one cent through the 30-minute high after 10:00, not a candle close above it.
questions.why: True. The trigger is a trade at least one cent above the 30-minute high after 10:00, a trade through and not a close. Trade-Ideas calls the breakout the first time price trades above that high, and Kullamagi enters on the opening range highs.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger is the trade through the range high, not a close.
questions.simple: True, because we buy when price trades through the high, and we do not wait for a candle to close.

reasons: fixed before (the lesson line was corrected on 2026-11-10)

questions.q: You are filled on the 10:00 break. Where does the stop go?
choices: A few cents under the day's low
Exactly on the 30-minute range low
A flat 3% under the price you paid
Halfway between the fill and the low
questions.answer: A few cents under the day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the day's low at the fill. On a first break after 10:00 that is normally the 30-minute low. UCT writes it as Stop LOD, and Kullamagi also says the stop is always the low of the day. Stop first, then size from it.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the day's low, then size from it.

wrong.Exactly on the 30-minute range low: The rule is a few cents under the low, not exactly on it.
wrong.A flat 3% under the price you paid: A percent is not a level. The stop is the day's low; about 3% is only where it usually lands.
wrong.Halfway between the fill and the low: A stop pulled in to fit is not the honest stop. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.

questions.simple: The stop goes a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it, and that low is normally the 30-minute low.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Never fill an ORB more than ___% above the 30-minute high.
questions.why: 4%. Never buy more than 4% above the buy point, and on an ORB the buy point is the 30-minute high. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the range, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. Past the line, wait for a pullback that holds, or a VWAP retest or undercut and hold mid morning.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the range high and we are done. A retest is the second chance.
questions.simple: We never buy more than 4% above the range high, because chasing pushes the stop farther away and shrinks the position.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)

questions.q: Bysshe picks swing candidates first, then uses the opening range to time the entry. Kullamagi also reads the setup off the daily chart.
questions.why: True. Bysshe says to identify candidates by your swing trade criteria and then use the opening range to time the entry. Kullamagi says to look at the daily chart and enter as the stock starts to break out. He adds that you need no intraday chart at all. These are two named authors' words, not a UCT rule.
questions.lesson_line: The setup lives on the daily chart. The opening range only times the buy.
questions.simple: True. Bysshe picks the candidates first, times the entry off the opening range, and Kullamagi also starts from the daily chart.

reasons: the parent-setup role is a held decision (D-002); keyed only as two authors' words

questions.q: The prior close is 48.10 and the 200-day sits at 52.40. At 10:05 the stock breaks its 30-minute high on big volume. Our rule?
choices: No long; the 200-day is the floor
Buy; big volume overrides the line
Buy half size, with a tight stop
No; buy it at the close instead
questions.answer: No long; the 200-day is the floor
questions.why: No long. The prior close is under the 200-day. The rule is no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long. It is a hard rule. The break and the volume do not change where the stock sits against the line.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day there is no ORB long to take. Volume does not vote.

wrong.Buy; big volume overrides the line: Nothing overrides the line except a parabolic long. A big-volume break is not one.
wrong.Buy half size, with a tight stop: Size does not fix a stock on the wrong side of the 200-day.
wrong.No; buy it at the close instead: A long at the close is still a long under the 200-day. The line, not the clock, is the test.

questions.simple: We do not buy a stock that sits under its 200-day line, however big the volume is.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: We take ORBs in leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in a strong group.
questions.why: True. Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups, except parabolic and mean-reversion trades. The ORB card asks the same. A clean break in a stock under that bar still fails the leader test.
questions.lesson_line: Leaders only. The range break is the timer, the RS is the ticket.
questions.simple: True. We take ORBs only in leaders, meaning an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)

questions.q: Kullamagi says that on a 60-minute chart the first candle is only 30 minutes, 9:30 to 10:00.
questions.why: True. Kullamagi writes that on the 60-minute timeframe the first candle is always only 30 minutes, 9:30 to 10:00. Trade-Ideas calls the first 30-minute candle of the day the opening range. We read our range on 30-minute bars, where the first candle is 9:30 to 10:00.
questions.lesson_line: Read the range on 30-minute bars. The first candle there is 9:30 to 10:00.
questions.simple: True. Kullamagi says the first candle on a 60-minute chart is only 30 minutes long, the same half hour as our range.

reworded: the old key False depended on how a platform cuts hourly candles

questions.q: At 10:03 a stock on your list prints a cent over its 30-minute high, with the 5-minute bar still open. Do you buy?
choices: Yes; the trade through is the trigger
No; wait for the 5-minute bar to close
No; wait for the 10:30 candle close
Yes, but only with a buy limit under it
questions.answer: Yes; the trade through is the trigger
questions.why: Yes. The trigger is a trade a cent or more above the 30-minute high after 10:00. It is a trade through, not a close. Entries are market orders. Waiting for a close can only mean a later fill. The fill still has to stay within 4% of the high.
questions.lesson_line: Set the alert at the range high. When it trades, you trade.

wrong.No; wait for the 5-minute bar to close: Our trigger is the trade through, not a close. Waiting only gives a later fill.
wrong.No; wait for the 10:30 candle close: The range closed at 10:00. The next trade through it is the trigger, whatever the clock.
wrong.Yes, but only with a buy limit under it: Entries are market orders. A buy limit under the price waits for a dip that may never come.

questions.simple: Yes, buy. The trigger is a trade through the high, not a close, and our entries are market orders.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57); order type is a held decision (D-038) that would not change the answer

questions.q: We may take an ORB in a $7 stock that trades $12 million a day.
questions.why: False. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one fails both tests: it costs $7 and trades $12 million. A clean range does not fix that.
questions.lesson_line: Price and dollar volume come before the chart. $10 and $20 million a day are the floor.
questions.simple: False. We trade only stocks priced at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: Before the open the 30-minute high does not exist yet. What goes in your written plan?
choices: A rule: a cent over the range high
A price guessed from the premarket
Nothing yet; just decide at 10:00 live
Yesterday's high as your buy level
questions.answer: A rule: a cent over the range high
questions.why: The rule. Every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens. The range is unknown until 10:00. So the plan reads: buy a cent over the 30-minute high. Put the stop a few cents under the day's low. Size from that distance.
questions.lesson_line: Write the rule, not the price. The range fills in the numbers at 10:00.

wrong.Nothing yet; just decide at 10:00 live: Every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the open. Deciding live skips the plan.
wrong.Yesterday's high as your buy level: That is the Kicker's other entry, not the ORB. The ORB buys the range high.
wrong.A price guessed from the premarket: Premarket is not the range. The rule waits for the real 30-minute high at 10:00.

questions.simple: Write a rule, not a price, because the range does not exist until 10:00.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D39)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The ORB trigger stays valid for the rest of that ___.
questions.why: Session. The trigger stays valid for the rest of that session. The 30-minute window is part of the trigger's definition, not a time-of-day rule. We have no time-of-day rule. A late break is still a break.
questions.lesson_line: The range sets the level, not a deadline. The break can come any time that day.
questions.simple: The word is session. The trigger stays good all day, because the 30 minutes only define it and are not a deadline.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C30)

questions.story: A leader on your focus list sets up for a Tuesday ORB. Its earnings report comes Thursday after the close, two sessions away.
questions.q: Take the break?
choices: No; a report inside 3 sessions
Yes; the stock is on the focus list
Yes, at half size with a tight stop
No; buy it at the close instead
questions.why: No. No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. A report on Thursday after the close puts a Tuesday buy inside that window. The day after the report is different: an ORB there is allowed.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings is a gap the stop cannot catch. Three sessions out, hands off.

wrong.Yes; the stock is on the focus list: The focus list does not override the earnings rule.
wrong.Yes, at half size with a tight stop: Half size is still a new buy inside the window.
wrong.No; buy it at the close instead: A buy at the close is still a new buy in the 3 sessions before the report.

questions.simple: No. We take no new buys in the 3 days before a report, and this report is two sessions away.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.story: The reading this morning is Orange. An A+ setup and a B setup on your list both break their 30-minute highs at 10:00.
questions.q: Which do you take?
choices: Only the A+; the B waits
Both; a break is a break
Neither; Orange means cash
Only the B; the A+ can wait
questions.answer: Only the A+; the B waits
questions.why: The A+ only. The market reading is a guide. Green is full risk, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange only A+ setups, Red mostly cash and shorts. Here it is Orange, so the B setup stays on the bench.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the range. Orange buys A+ and nothing else.

wrong.Both; a break is a break: Orange narrows you to A+. The B setup waits for a better market.
wrong.Neither; Orange means cash: Red is mostly cash. Orange still allows the best setups.
wrong.Only the B; the A+ can wait: Orange allows only A+ setups. The A+ does not wait; the B does.

questions.simple: Take the A+ only. In an Orange market we buy only A+ setups, so the B waits.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)
fixed before

questions.q: The 30-minute high is 418.45 and the low 412.06. You fill at 418.46 with the stop at 412.01. How far below the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 1.54%. Take the fill minus the stop, 418.46 minus 412.01, and divide by the fill. That was FFIV's stop, a few cents under the range low. It sits inside the 3% a stop usually stays within, and it sets the size.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: The stop is about 1.54% below the fill: the fill minus the stop, divided by the fill.

reasons: computed key
3% stop width is a held decision (D-005); only A13's 'usually about 3%' is used

questions.q: On a Kicker ORB the stop is capped at 3.5% under the entry, and Kickers usually need a wider stop than that.
questions.why: False. The 3.5% cap is real: on a Kicker the stop is the Kicker low or 3.5% under the entry, whichever is closer. But we should usually get these with a stop smaller than 3.5%. So a wider stop is not the usual need.
questions.lesson_line: On a Kicker ORB the stop is capped at 3.5%, or the Kicker low if closer.
questions.simple: False, because Kickers usually fit a stop smaller than the 3.5% cap, so they do not need a wider one.

deeper.example: On JBI the ORB entry filled at 11.21, and 3.5% under that is 10.82, the Kicker low itself. So the cap and the low gave the same stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's 2026-11-02 Kicker ruling (v03)
fixed before (lesson line corrected)

questions.q: A Kicker ORB fills at 11.21. Where is the stop under the 3.5% cap?
questions.why: 10.82. The fill times one minus 3.5%: 11.21 x 0.965. On a Kicker the stop is the Kicker low or 3.5% under the entry, whichever is closer. On JBI the cap landed on the Kicker low itself, so the cap and the low agreed.
questions.lesson_line: Know the cap before the fill. 3.5% under the entry, or the Kicker low, whichever is closer.
questions.simple: Take 3.5% off the fill of 11.21 and the stop is 10.82, or the Kicker low if that is closer.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's Kicker ruling (2026-11-02)

questions.story: A Kicker opens below the red day's high of 11.04. At 9:41 it trades through 11.04. The first 30-minute candle later tops near 11.20.
questions.q: Which entry fills first?
choices: The prior-day-high buy fills first
The ORB buy; it is the only entry
Neither; nothing fills before 10:00
Both, with the size split in two
questions.why: The prior-day-high buy. On a Kicker you can buy the opening range break or the break of the previous day's high. When it opens below that high, the previous-day-high order comes first and is cheaper. The ORB is the confirmation entry, and it can only fill after 10:00.
questions.lesson_line: Opens under the red day's high: the high is the first entry, the ORB confirms it.

wrong.The ORB buy; it is the only entry: The Kicker has two entries. The ORB is the second when it opens under the red day's high.
wrong.Neither; nothing fills before 10:00: The prior-day-high trigger needs no range. It fires the moment 11.04 trades.
wrong.Both, with the size split in two: The plan is full size at one price with one stop. Two entries are a choice, not a split.

questions.simple: The prior-day-high buy fills first, because the stock opens below that high and the ORB comes later as the confirmation.

deeper.example: JBI, 2023-12-14: it opened below the red day's high. The previous-day-high entry filled at 11.05 with a stop at 10.80, 2.3% away. The ORB entry filled at 11.21, 3.7% from the same stop. At the close the first was up about 2.3R and the ORB about 1.0R.

reasons: the Kicker entry order is a proposed card line backed by the JBI example and the owner's Kicker ruling

questions.q: An ORB stop stays in your head until the first trim, then goes in as a real broker order.
questions.why: False. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. That holds before the first trim too. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule.
questions.lesson_line: Every position has a real stop order with the broker. Never a stop in your head.
questions.simple: False. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, never a stop kept in your head.

reasons: rests on the account rulebook D41 and A4

questions.q: Your ORB long is up 2R by noon. By the hard rule, when does the first third come off?
choices: At 3R
Now, at 2R
At 5R
At the close
questions.why: At 3R. One R is the fill minus the stop, your risk per share. The hard rule is a third at 3R. After that, another third comes off at 5R and the last third trails. At 2R nothing is sold yet: the stop may go to breakeven anywhere from 2R to 5R.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R, a third at 5R, trail the rest. 2R is where breakeven may start.

wrong.Now, at 2R: 2R is the earliest the stop moves to breakeven, not a trim level.
wrong.At 5R: 5R is the second third. The hard rule trims the first at 3R.
wrong.At the close: Crabel exited at the close, and that is not ours. Our trims are set by R levels.

questions.simple: The first third comes off at 3R by the hard rule. At 2R the stop may go to breakeven, but nothing is sold.

deeper.trap: Do not mix the hard rule with a habit. The rulebook says the first trim can ideally come anywhere from 3R to 6R. The hard rule, the one a written plan can state, is a third at 3R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)
fixed before

questions.story: Your Kicker plan reads: buy the 30-minute ORB. The red day's low is 24.10. Premarket the stock trades 23.80.
questions.q: Does the ORB plan stand?
choices: No; the Kicker setup is broken
Yes; wait for 10:00 as planned
Yes, if the stock reclaims 24.10
No; buy the prior-day high instead
questions.answer: No; the Kicker setup is broken
questions.why: No. Before the fill, a trade under the red day's low breaks the Kicker, and 23.80 is under 24.10. The ORB was only the Kicker's timer, so with no setup there is no trade. The prior-day-high entry belongs to the same Kicker and goes with it.
questions.lesson_line: No daily setup, no ORB. The timer has nothing left to time.

wrong.Yes; wait for 10:00 as planned: The plan rode on the Kicker. Under the red day's low there is no Kicker.
wrong.Yes, if the stock reclaims 24.10: A trade under 24.10 voids the plan before the fill. No reclaim exception is taught.
wrong.No; buy the prior-day high instead: The prior-day-high buy is the Kicker's other entry. A trade under the red day's low breaks the Kicker, so both entries go with it.

questions.simple: No, because the stock traded under the red day's low, so the Kicker is broken and the ORB has nothing to time.

reasons: rests on the rulebook's no setup, no trade (D44) and the card's parent-broken line (c10, a proposal)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: After the fill, a big-volume reversal back into the range is a ___, not a second exit rule.
questions.why: A warning. After the fill the stop decides. A big-volume reversal back into the range is the classic failure shape and worth watching, but it is not a second exit rule. The stop is the exit, and it only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Watch the reversal, honour the stop. One exit rule, not two.
questions.simple: A big-volume reversal back into the range is only a warning, because after the fill the stop is the only exit.

reasons: rests on the rulebook A4 and the card's settled line (c11)

questions.q: Fill 146.91, stop 143.86. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 156.06. One R is the fill minus the stop. Add three of those to the fill of 146.91 and you reach 156.06. The first third comes off there. ANF got there in about three sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R the moment you are filled. The first third comes off there.
questions.simple: One R is the fill minus the stop, so 3R is the fill plus three of those, which is 156.06.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)

questions.q: The 30-minute high is 60.91. You look up at 10:20 and the stock trades 63.60. How far above the high is that, in percent?
questions.why: 4.42%, past the 4% line. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the range, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. Pass and wait for a pullback that holds or a VWAP retest.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the chase before you buy it. Past 4%, wait for the pullback.
questions.simple: The stock is 4.42% above the high, which is past the 4% limit, so we pass.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)

questions.story: You missed the 10:00 break. At 10:25 the stock is 6% above its 30-minute high and still climbing.
questions.q: What now?
choices: Wait for a retest of the high
Buy now; the momentum is proof
Buy half size just to be in
Forget it; a missed break is gone
questions.answer: Wait for a retest of the high
questions.why: Wait for a retest of the high. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point, and this stock is 6% over its range high. If you miss the break, look for a pullback to the range high that holds. We also look for a VWAP retest, or an undercut and hold, mid morning. Steenbarger likes the first pullback after a valid break too, once buying resumes.
questions.lesson_line: Past 4%, do not chase. Wait for the pullback that holds.

wrong.Buy now; the momentum is proof: Six percent over the high is past the 4% line. Bysshe: you buy too far from the right entry.
wrong.Buy half size just to be in: Half of a chase is still a chase. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows.
wrong.Forget it; a missed break is gone: A miss is not final. We look for a pullback to the range high that holds, or a VWAP retest mid morning.

questions.simple: Wait for a pullback that holds, because a price 6% over the high is past our 4% chase limit.

deeper.trap: A stock that keeps climbing makes the chase feel safe. But chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. Past 4% over the high, the retest is your second chance, not a miss.

reasons: rests on rulebook C28 (4%) and the owner's VWAP alternative (u01)
fixed before (a wrong choice was shortened)

questions.story: You bought the ORB at 274.04 with the stop at 270.67. A third came off at 3R and the stop moved to breakeven. Three sessions later a report gaps it open under 270.67.
questions.q: What is the stop now?
choices: The low of the first 30 minutes
The gap-down day's opening price
Breakeven, where it already sat
A flat 3% under the open price
questions.answer: The low of the first 30 minutes
questions.why: The first 30-minute low. A gap against the stop hands the decision to the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day. The low of that first 30-minute bar is the new stop. It is the one exception to a stop that only moves up. There is a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide, under a 2R ceiling.

wrong.The gap-down day's opening price: The gap rule gives the decision to the first 30 minutes. The open is not the new stop.
wrong.Breakeven, where it already sat: Price is already through breakeven. The gap rule makes the first 30-minute low the new stop.
wrong.A flat 3% under the open price: A percent is not a level. The gap rule names the first 30-minute low, under a 2R ceiling.

questions.simple: The new stop is the low of the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day. If that loss passes 2R, you leave.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)
fixed before

questions.q: On an ORB winner the stop stays at the first stop until the last third is sold.
questions.why: False. The stop goes to breakeven somewhere from 2R to 5R, ideally. The stop only moves up, and it does not sit at the first stop until the last third is sold.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R. The stop only moves up.
questions.simple: False. Breakeven comes somewhere from 2R to 5R, ideally, so the stop does not wait for the last third.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19)
the 'first trim by default' half is the card's line
fixed before

questions.story: Stopped out of the ORB at 10:40, your first stop-out on this stock this week. At 11:15 the stock retakes the day's high.
questions.q: Can you buy again?
choices: Yes; a new trade, and it counts
No; the limit is one try a day
Yes, and reuse the old stop level
No; wait for tomorrow's range
questions.answer: Yes; a new trade, and it counts
questions.why: Yes. A retake of the day's high after a stop-out is a new trigger with a new stop. You buy it as a new trade, under every rule. It counts against the 3 tries a week and 6 a month on that stock.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a verdict. The retake is a new trade with its own stop, and it counts.

wrong.No; the limit is one try a day: The limit is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month, not one a day.
wrong.No; wait for tomorrow's range: The retake of the day's high is the trigger. Tomorrow has its own range.
wrong.Yes, and reuse the old stop level: A new trade has its own stop under its own low. The old stop is gone.

questions.simple: Yes. A retake of the day's high is a new trade with its own stop, and it uses one of your tries.

reasons: rests on rulebook B21 and E56

questions.q: Average daily volume is 3,000,000 shares. What is the most we would own?
choices: 30,000 shares, 1% of the volume
3,000 shares, 0.1% of the volume
300,000 shares, 10% of the volume
No limit if the stop is tight
questions.why: 30,000 shares. Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume: 3,000,000 x 1% is 30,000. The rule has no exception for a tight stop. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume, and not a share more.

wrong.3,000 shares, 0.1% of the volume: That is far under the ceiling, not the most. The ceiling is 1% of the average volume.
wrong.300,000 shares, 10% of the volume: That is ten times the ceiling. The rule is 1%.
wrong.No limit if the stop is tight: The rule has no exception for a tight stop. The ceiling stands.

questions.simple: We may own at most 1% of the average daily volume, so with 3,000,000 shares traded that is 30,000 shares.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

questions.story: 9:50. The stock on your list is ripping, already above its 9:30 to 9:45 high on big volume. The plan says 30-minute ORB.
questions.q: Buy now?
choices: No; the range is set at 10:00
Yes; it is running on volume
Yes, half now, half at 10:00
No; the plan is void for the day
questions.answer: No; the range is set at 10:00
questions.why: No. The 30-minute range is the day's high and low at 10:00, so the trigger does not exist at 9:50. Buying before 10:00 because the stock is running is a named mistake: the ORB waits for the range.
questions.lesson_line: The first minutes are not the trade. The range is, and it closes at 10:00.

wrong.Yes; it is running on volume: Running is why it is tempting. The trigger does not exist until the range closes.
wrong.Yes, half now, half at 10:00: Full size at one price. Half a plan is no plan.
wrong.No; the plan is void for the day: Nothing is void. The plan waits for 10:00 like it said.

questions.simple: No, because the range is not set until 10:00, and buying early because a stock is running is a known mistake.

deeper.trap: Half now, half at 10:00 feels like a fair compromise, but it is two entries at two prices. The rule is full size at one price with one stop, and before 10:00 there is no trigger at all.

reasons: rests on the card's named mistake (c27, a proposal)

questions.story: Same stock, same range, same volume. One day the break comes at 10:00. Another day it comes at 10:50.
questions.q: Is the 10:50 break a valid trigger?
choices: Yes; we have no time-of-day rule
No; it is too late in the morning
Only if it breaks before 10:30
Yes, but only at half the size
questions.answer: Yes; we have no time-of-day rule
questions.why: Yes. We have no time-of-day rule. The 30-minute window defines the trigger, and the trigger stays valid for the rest of that session. QLYS triggered at 10:50 and reached 5R in three sessions.
questions.lesson_line: A late break is still a break. The clock sets the range, not a deadline.

wrong.No; it is too late in the morning: The range closed at 10:00. A break counts whenever it comes that session.
wrong.Only if it breaks before 10:30: Nothing in the rules sets a cut-off. The window defines the trigger, not a deadline.
wrong.Yes, but only at half the size: Size comes from the risk and the stop, not the clock.

questions.simple: Yes, a 10:50 break counts. We have no time-of-day rule, and the trigger lasts all session.

deeper.counter: A late trigger is valid, not a promise. QLYS broke at 10:50, reached 5R in three sessions, then fell all the way back to the stop by session 10. Selling a third at 3R and another at 5R is how a run like that is kept.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C30)
fixed before

questions.story: A leader sits above its 200-day but under its 50-day after a six-week slide. It breaks its 30-minute high at 10:05 on 2x opening volume.
questions.q: Take it as an ORB on our card?
choices: Pass; it is under the 50-day
Take it; the 200-day is enough
Take it; the 2x volume decides
Take it, but with a wider stop
questions.why: Pass. Our card wants the prior close above the 50-day simple moving average, as well as above the 200-day. This leader is above its 200-day but under its 50-day. Bysshe likewise asks for a positive daily trend, with rising 20 and 50-day averages.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200 is the floor. Above the 50 is the trend. The ORB wants both.

wrong.Take it; the 200-day is enough: The 200-day is the hard floor. The card adds the 50-day for the trend, and this stock fails it.
wrong.Take it; the 2x volume decides: Volume does not fix a stock under its 50-day.
wrong.Take it, but with a wider stop: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low and only moves up, never wider. A wider stop does not fix a failed line.

questions.simple: Pass, because our card also wants the stock above its 50-day, and this one is under it.

reasons: the 50-day line is the card's proposed criterion, not the rulebook's
fixed before

questions.q: Two thirds of an ORB winner are sold at 3R and 5R. What takes you out of the last third?
choices: A close under the 10 or 21-day
A touch of the 30-minute low
The next earnings report
A fixed 10R, whatever the chart
questions.why: A close under the trail line. After the thirds at 3R and 5R, the last third trails: the 10-day average for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones. We sell on a close below it.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the rising average. Sell the close below it, not the touch.

wrong.A touch of the 30-minute low: That was the first day's stop. By the trail stage the stop is at breakeven or higher.
wrong.The next earnings report: Hold through a report only if up 5R. That is a separate rule, not the trail.
wrong.A fixed 10R, whatever the chart: The last third trails the average. The ladder names no fixed 10R exit.

questions.simple: Sell the last third on a close below the 10-day or 21-day average, not on a touch.

reasons: rests on rulebook E52 and E51 (E51 is marked adjustable)

questions.q: An ORB trade still under 1R after ten sessions gets a month more before it is closed.
questions.why: False. Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. Ten sessions is the limit, not a month. The rule is about a trade stuck under 1R.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.
questions.simple: False. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, not held for another month.

reasons: one cited fact only (C33)
rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.story: Your ORB long closed Monday at 2.7R. Tuesday it gaps open at 3.5R.
questions.q: By the hard rule, when does the first trim come off?
choices: At the open; the level is passed
Wait for a dip back to the level
At the close, once it settles
Not yet; hold out for 5R
questions.answer: At the open; the level is passed
questions.why: At the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open. It opened at 3.5R, past the 3R level, so the first third comes off right there. The next third waits for 5R.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through a trim level is the trim. Take it at the open.

wrong.At the close, once it settles: The rule says take it at the open, not the close.
wrong.Wait for a dip back to the level: It opened at 3.5R, already past the 3R level. The rule is to take the trim at the open, not to wait for a dip.
wrong.Not yet; hold out for 5R: A third at 3R is the hard rule. 5R is where the second third comes off.

questions.simple: Sell the first third at the open, since the stock opened past 3R. The next third waits for 5R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63)
fixed before

questions.story: You are filled on the 10:00 break and the stock is moving your way. You are writing the exit plan.
questions.q: What is our exit?
choices: A third at 3R and 5R, trail the rest
Sell it all at twice the range height
Flat at the close of the first day
A third to a half after 3 to 5 days
questions.answer: A third at 3R and 5R, trail the rest
questions.why: A third at 3R, a third at 5R, and trail the last third. Not ours: a target of twice the range, Crabel's first-day close exit, and Kullamagi's sale after 3 to 5 days. We swing trade and sell by R, not by the calendar. The 5R step is adjustable.
questions.lesson_line: Same trigger, different trade. Our exit is the R ladder and the trail.

wrong.A third to a half after 3 to 5 days: That is Kullamagi's sale. Ours sells by R, not by the calendar.
wrong.Sell it all at twice the range height: A target of twice the range is not our exit.
wrong.Flat at the close of the first day: Crabel usually took profits at the first day's close or the first profitable close. We sell by R and hold the ones that work.

questions.simple: We sell a third at 3R, another third at 5R, and trail the last third, by R and not by the calendar.

reasons: rests on rulebook B19 and E51; the others' exits are cited as theirs

questions.q: Which kind of day before the open grades an ORB higher?
choices: A quiet, tight inside day
A wide-range expansion day
An ordinary day with no pattern
A climax day on huge volume
questions.why: A quiet, tight inside day. Contraction the day before is a cue: an inside day, an NR4 or NR7 day, or a tight base. Crabel's hypothesis is that inside days precede trend days and successful opening range breakouts. It is a cue, not a fixed checklist.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet before the open, loud after it. Contraction is the cue.

wrong.A wide-range expansion day: The opposite. The cue is contraction the day before, not expansion.
wrong.A climax day on huge volume: A climax is a big move on big volume. The cue is contraction the day before.
wrong.An ordinary day with no pattern: An ordinary day shows no cue. The cue is contraction: an inside day, an NR4 or NR7 day, or a tight base.

questions.simple: A tight inside day is the cue, since Crabel's idea is that inside days come before trend days and good breakouts.

reasons: the cue is the card's proposal and the rulebook says grading is discretionary (E50)
Crabel's line is a hypothesis from a publisher's abstract
fixed before

questions.q: Account 100,000. On this trade you risk 0.25%. Fill 274.04, stop 270.67. How many shares?
questions.why: 74 shares. Shares = account x risk % / (entry - stop), rounded down, then capped. Here that is 100,000 x 0.25% divided by 274.04 minus 270.67, which rounds down to 74. The 40% position cap does not bind here. The stop sets the size.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size, never the other way round.
questions.simple: Risk dollars divided by the gap between the fill and the stop, rounded down, gives 74 shares.

deeper.trap: The cap can bind. Risk a larger percent on the same trade and the risk-based size can pass the position cap of 40% of the account. The size is then the smaller of the two.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7)
changed 2026-11-10 (risk 1% to 0.25%)

questions.story: At 10:00 the range is 4.55% wide on 2.7x opening volume, RS 92. The break fills at 185.11; a few cents under the low is 176.63, 4.58% away.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Pass; the honest stop does not fit
Pass; heavy volume is a red flag here
Pull the stop in to a flat 3% loss
Buy; the heavy volume carries it
questions.answer: Pass; the honest stop does not fit
questions.why: Pass. Stop first; the size comes from the stop. The stop here is 4.58% under the fill, and we almost never take a loss past 3% on a position. Cutting the size does not shrink that loss on the position. If the honest stop does not fit, skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop inside the noise.

wrong.Pass; heavy volume is a red flag here: Heavy opening volume is a grade cue, not a reason to skip. The reason to pass is the honest stop.
wrong.Pull the stop in to a flat 3% loss: A stop pulled in to 3% sits above the day's low, inside the range. It is no longer the honest stop.
wrong.Buy; the heavy volume carries it: Volume grades the day. It does not shrink a 4.58% stop. GKOS reached 0.33R and was stopped.

questions.simple: Pass. The honest stop is 4.58% away, past our usual 3%, and we do not squeeze a stop to make a trade fit.

reasons: rests on rulebook A3 and A13 (h04), with the stop-width decision (D-005) still pending
the 4.58% comes from one dossier scan row

questions.story: You bought the 10:00 break at 46.37 with the stop at 45.51. By 10:30 it is back inside the range, under VWAP, still above your stop.
questions.q: What now?
choices: Hold; the stop is the exit
Sell now; the reversal says so
Move the stop lower to give it room
Hold, but sell it at the close
questions.answer: Hold; the stop is the exit
questions.why: Hold. After the fill the stop decides. Even a big-volume reversal back into the range is the classic failure shape, a warning to watch, not a second exit rule. The stop only moves up. APA, with these numbers, took its stop at 12:45 the same day, a planned loss.
questions.lesson_line: The warning tells you to watch. The stop tells you when to leave.

wrong.Sell now; the reversal says so: The reversal is a warning, not a second exit rule. The stop is the exit, and it sits with the broker as a real order.
wrong.Hold, but sell it at the close: Crabel's exit at the close is not ours. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Move the stop lower to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.

questions.simple: Hold, because after the fill the stop decides, and the reversal is only a warning to watch.

deeper.example: APA, 2026-09-14: a 2.3% gap above the prior day's high on 1.7x opening volume, RS 90. The break ran 0.26R, fell back through the range high by 10:30, lost VWAP and took the stop at 12:45. The loss stayed at 1R because the stop sat under the day's low.

reasons: rests on rulebook A4 and the card's settled line (c11)

questions.story: You bought the 10:30 break at 64.43, stop 63.21. It reaches 5R in session 7, then slides all the way back to 63.21 by session 18.
questions.q: By our rules, what did you keep?
choices: Two thirds banked, the rest trailed
Nothing; it came back to the stop
One third banked, the rest stopped
Half banked at 2R, the rest on a trail
questions.answer: Two thirds banked, the rest trailed
questions.why: Two thirds banked. A third comes off at 3R and another at 5R. The stop goes to breakeven at the first trim by default, and the last third trails. OVV hit 5R in session 7, so both trims were in before it slid back to 63.21 in session 18.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength. The trims are what you keep when the move gives it all back.

wrong.Nothing; it came back to the stop: Only if nothing was sold and the stop never moved. Our plan sold two thirds on the way up.
wrong.One third banked, the rest stopped: 5R in session 7 means the second third came off at 5R too. Two trims were banked before the slide.
wrong.Half banked at 2R, the rest on a trail: 2R is where breakeven may start, not a trim. The trims are a third at 3R and a third at 5R.

questions.simple: You keep two thirds, because the thirds sold at 3R and 5R are banked even if the rest slides back.

reasons: rests on rulebook B19 and E51 (the 5R step is adjustable)
the session counts come from one dossier scan row

questions.q: The ORB entry is a market order as price trades through the 30-minute high.
questions.why: True. Entries are market orders. When price trades through the range high, you buy at market, and the stop order goes to the broker.
questions.lesson_line: Market order on the trade through the high. Stop order with the broker.
questions.simple: True, because all our entries are market orders, so we buy at market once price trades through the high.

reasons: rests on rulebook E57; a buy-stop (D-038, pending) would not change this answer

questions.story: A clean 10:00 break on 2.1x opening volume, the range high over the prior day's high, no report near. The RS rating is 64.
questions.q: Take it?
choices: Pass; RS 64 is not a leader
Pass; revisit it on the retest
Take it; the break is clean
Take it; volume beats RS
questions.answer: Pass; RS 64 is not a leader
questions.why: Pass. We buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. This stock's RS is 64. DHR's break was clean, yet it reached only 0.58R before the stop. A clean break does not make a laggard a leader.
questions.lesson_line: A clean break in a laggard is a laggard having a good morning.

wrong.Take it; the break is clean: The chart is one gate. RS is another, and 64 fails it.
wrong.Take it; volume beats RS: Volume grades the day. It never substitutes for leadership.
wrong.Pass; revisit it on the retest: A retest changes the price, not the RS. A laggard is still a laggard on the second try.

questions.simple: Pass. An RS rating of 64 is under our line of 80, so it is not a leader, however clean the break.

reasons: rests on rulebook C31; the RS in the example is a proxy rank

questions.story: A leader pulls back to its 20-day EMA. On the 30-minute chart four red candles, then a green one at 11:00. The buy is over that green candle's high, well under the morning high.
questions.q: Which trade is that?
choices: A 30-minute pivot trade
An ORB, the 10:00 break
An opening drive entry
A retest of the range high
questions.why: A 30-minute pivot. It buys the high of the first green 30-minute candle after a string of red ones at a daily level. That level usually sits well below the morning high. An ORB buys the first trade through the first half hour's high after 10:00. A drive is bought over the first 5-minute bar's high by about 9:40.
questions.lesson_line: Find the level being bought. The range high is the ORB; the turn candle's high is the pivot.

wrong.An ORB, the 10:00 break: The ORB's level is the first half hour's high. This buy sits well under it, at a turn candle.
wrong.An opening drive entry: A drive is bought over the first bar's high in the opening minutes. This is an 11:00 turn after a pullback.
wrong.A retest of the range high: A retest buys the pullback to the range high after a break. This buy sits well under the morning high, at a turn candle.

questions.simple: It is a 30-minute pivot, because the buy is over the first green candle after red ones, well under the morning high.

deeper.trap: The tell is the level and the clock. The ORB buys the first half hour's high after 10:00. The pivot buys a turn candle's high at a daily level, here the 20-day EMA, usually well below the morning high. Same chart, different level.

reasons: one cited fact only defines the pivot (c19)
the lookalike tells are the card's proposals, not owner rulings

questions.story: A stock gaps up 2% and runs from the bell. At 9:36 the buy fires over the first 5-minute bar's high; the day's low is inside that bar.
questions.q: Which trade is that?
choices: An opening drive
A 30-minute ORB
A 30-minute pivot
A VWAP retest buy
questions.why: An opening drive. It sets the day's low in the first 5-minute bar and is bought over that bar's high by about 9:40. An ORB waits for the full 30-minute range and buys after 10:00.
questions.lesson_line: Name the drive: its low is set in the first 5-minute bar, and it is bought by about 9:40.

wrong.A 30-minute ORB: The range does not exist until 10:00. A 9:36 buy is the drive, the fast version.
wrong.A 30-minute pivot: A pivot needs a string of red candles into a level first. This is straight up from the bell.
wrong.A VWAP retest buy: A VWAP retest or undercut-and-hold is a mid morning buy after a dip. This one is straight up from the bell, with no dip.

questions.simple: It is an opening drive, because the buy fires over the first 5-minute bar's high at 9:36, before any 30-minute range exists.

deeper.trap: The clock is the tell. Before 10:00 no 30-minute range exists, so a buy at 9:36 cannot be our ORB, however strong the stock. The drive trades the first 5-minute bar; the ORB waits for the full range and buys after 10:00.

reasons: one cited fact only defines the drive (c20)
the lookalike tells are the card's proposals, not owner rulings

questions.story: A stock gaps up 3% and breaks its 30-minute high at 10:00. The day before the gap was a doji, not a red day.
questions.q: What is it?
choices: A plain gap ORB, no Kicker
A Kicker ORB after the doji
An EP, a gap on a catalyst
An opening drive, bought late
questions.answer: A plain gap ORB, no Kicker
questions.why: A plain gap ORB. A Kicker needs a real red day before the gap, and a doji before it makes a plain gap ORB. An EP needs a gap of 10% or more on a named catalyst, and this one is 3%.
questions.lesson_line: Look at yesterday. A doji is not a red day, so there is no Kicker.

wrong.A Kicker ORB after the doji: A Kicker needs a real red day before the gap, and a doji is not one.
wrong.An EP, a gap on a catalyst: An EP opens 10% or more on a named catalyst. A 3% gap is far short of that.
wrong.An opening drive, bought late: A drive is bought over the first 5-minute bar's high by about 9:40. This break came at 10:00 over the 30-minute high, so it is an ORB.

questions.simple: It is a plain gap ORB. A Kicker needs a real red day before the gap, and a doji is not one.

deeper.trap: Two checks: the day before, and the size of the gap. A Kicker needs a real red day first; a doji or a green day makes a plain gap ORB. An EP needs a gap of 10% or more on a named catalyst. A 3% gap after a doji is neither.

reasons: rests on the card's lookalike rows (c21, c22), proposals and not rulings
the card's 'not traded alone' line (c28, D-002) is no longer keyed

questions.story: A stock gaps 12% on earnings news. The first 30-minute range runs 7% from low to high. At 10:10 it trades through the high.
questions.q: What is it, for our rules?
choices: An EP day; the stop sets the size
An ordinary ORB; buy the break
A Kicker; cap the stop at 3.5%
A gap ORB; pull the stop in to 3%
questions.answer: An EP day; the stop sets the size
questions.why: An EP day. An EP opens 10% or more above the prior close on a named catalyst. Its 30-minute range is usually too wide for a 3% stop. Here the gap is 12% and the range runs 7%. The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, and it sets the size. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the gap and the range. A 7% range is not a 3% stop.

wrong.An ordinary ORB; buy the break: A 12% gap on news is the EP's test, not the ORB's. The range alone is wider than our usual stop.
wrong.A Kicker; cap the stop at 3.5%: A Kicker needs a real red day before the gap, and none is given. This is a 12% news gap.
wrong.A gap ORB; pull the stop in to 3%: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low. Pulling it in to 3% inside a 7% range is not the honest stop.

questions.simple: An EP day: a 12% gap on news. The range is wider than a usual 3% stop, so the stop sets the size.

deeper.trap: Do not shrink the stop to make the trade fit. The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, and a stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip.

reasons: the key rests on one card line (c22)
stop width is a held decision (D-005)
fixed before

questions.story: Two 10:00 breaks in leaders, each with the range high above yesterday's high. One came on opening volume about normal, 1.03x. The other came on 2.67x.
questions.q: Which grades higher?
choices: The 2.67x break; a crowd is in
The 1.03x break; quiet is better
Equal; only the break matters
Neither; wait for a retest first
questions.answer: The 2.67x break; a crowd is in
questions.why: The 2.67x break. A stock in play, with a catalyst and heavy opening volume, is a grade cue. Bysshe's best clue is volume, and Kullamagi's best gaps trade their average daily volume early. IQV, a 1.03x break, was an ordinary day and was stopped. No fixed volume line is taught as ours.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy opening volume is the crowd showing up. It is a cue, not a rule.

wrong.The 1.03x break; quiet is better: Quiet belongs to the day before the open, where contraction is the cue. On the open itself we want a crowd. IQV reached 1.29R and was stopped.
wrong.Equal; only the break matters: The break is the trigger. The volume and the context are the grade.
wrong.Neither; wait for a retest first: The trigger is the trade through the high, not a retest. A retest is the second chance when you miss the first.

questions.simple: The 2.67x break grades higher, because heavy opening volume is a cue that a stock is in play.

deeper.example: IQV: a quiet break at 10:00 with no opening interest behind it, opening volume 1.03x its 20-day mean. It reached 1.29R and was stopped. FFIV, by contrast, broke on 2.67x opening volume and ran 10.05R.

reasons: the volume line (D-006) is pending and never keyed
the cue is the card's proposal and E50 says grading is discretionary

questions.story: 10:15, and the reading is Green. The indexes are taking out their own opening ranges on buying. Three of your best setups sit at their range highs.
questions.q: What does that mean for those setups?
choices: Execute the focus-list breaks
Buy the index instead of the names
Wait for the close to decide
Nothing; indexes are not a cue
questions.why: Execute. We look for buying and opening ranges taken out, or strong hourly candles after the first 30 minutes. Then we can execute on our focus list. The index break is the cue. The names are the trades. Each name still buys on its own trade through its range high.
questions.lesson_line: When the indexes clear their ranges, the focus list gets the green light.

wrong.Wait for the close to decide: The cue comes after the first 30 minutes, and it is already 10:15. Waiting for the close skips the trigger.
wrong.Nothing; indexes are not a cue: They are the cue. Our notes name the indexes taking out their opening ranges as the sign to execute the list.
wrong.Buy the index instead of the names: The cue says execute on the focus list. The index break is the cue; the names are the trades.

questions.simple: Execute the focus-list breaks. When the indexes take out their opening ranges on buying, that is our cue.

deeper.trap: A cue is not a trigger. The indexes clearing their ranges says the list can go. Each name still needs its own trade through its range high, with its own stop.

reasons: the index cue is a proposed card line plus the owner's published note
fixed before

questions.q: Bought at 60.92, stop 59.51. The stock trades to 67.97. How many R is that?
questions.why: 5R. One R is the fill minus the stop. The move from 60.92 to 67.97 is five of those. That is where the second third comes off, after the first at 3R. EXEL's trigger fill was 60.92, and it reached 9.06R in the window we read.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. 5R is the second trim.
questions.simple: The stock is up 5R, because the gain from the fill is five times the risk per share.

deeper.example: Same trade, first trim: 3R is the fill plus three times the risk per share, and a third comes off there. The second third waits for 67.97, which is 5R, and the last third trails.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (E51)

questions.story: The reading is Red. A leader on your list breaks its 30-minute high at 10:00 on three times normal volume.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Skip it; mostly cash and shorts
Buy it; A+ setups trade anywhere
Buy it at half size, tight stop
No; buy it at the close instead
questions.answer: Skip it; mostly cash and shorts
questions.why: No long. In a Red market: mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day. The market reading is a guide: Green is full risk, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange only A+, Red mostly cash and shorts. A strong break does not change the reading.
questions.lesson_line: The market reading comes before the range. Red means sit on your hands.

wrong.Buy it; A+ setups trade anywhere: Orange allows only A+ setups. Red is mostly cash and shorts, so a long is out.
wrong.Buy it at half size, tight stop: Half size is not a reading. Red is mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day.
wrong.No; buy it at the close instead: A buy at the close is still a long in a Red market. The reading, not the clock, is the test.

questions.simple: Skip the long. In a Red market we hold mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day.

deeper.trap: The best-looking break in a Red market is the test of the reading. Three times normal volume makes the long tempting, but Red means mostly cash, plus shorts below the 200-day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65, D46)
fixed before

questions.story: Your ORB long is up 2.2R. The company reports tomorrow before the open.
questions.q: Hold through it?
choices: No; hold through only if up 5R
Yes, after selling half first
Yes; move the stop to breakeven
No; hold through only if up 3R
questions.answer: No; hold through only if up 5R
questions.why: No. Hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R, and this one is up 2.2R, so it does not qualify. A stop cannot catch an overnight gap: SNX's report of 2026-09-24 gapped it straight through the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings is a gap you cannot stop. Five R buys the ticket; 2.2R does not.

wrong.Yes; move the stop to breakeven: A stop cannot catch an overnight gap. Breakeven is not protection here.
wrong.Yes, after selling half first: Half of a 2.2R cushion is still under the 5R line.
wrong.No; hold through only if up 3R: 3R is where the first third comes off. The line for holding through a report is 5R.

questions.simple: No. We hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R, and this one is up just 2.2R.

deeper.trap: An earnings gap is the one move a stop cannot cap, so a stop is no protection here. SNX's report of 2026-09-24 gapped it through the stop, and the thirds sold at 3R and 5R are what kept the win. Selling half or moving the stop to breakeven does not change the 5R line.

reasons: rests on rulebook B22 (5R)
the rule does not say whether to sell all or trim

questions.story: JBI, a Kicker. The prior-day-high entry fills at 11.05; the ORB entry fills at 11.21. Both use the stop under the Kicker low, 10.80.
questions.q: Which entry sits closer to the stop?
choices: The 11.05 entry, the earlier fill
The 11.21 entry, once confirmed
Both the same, with the same stop
The 11.21 entry; it has more room
questions.why: The 11.05 entry. Its stop sits 2.3% away; the ORB entry at 11.21 has 3.7% to the same stop. A tighter stop buys more shares for the same dollar risk. At the close the first was up about 2.3R, the ORB about 1.0R.
questions.lesson_line: Same stop, two entries. The earlier one sits closer, so the stop is tighter and the size can be bigger.

wrong.The 11.21 entry, once confirmed: Confirmation costs distance. The ORB entry fills at 11.21, which is 3.7% from the same stop.
wrong.Both the same, with the same stop: The same stop with a higher fill is a wider stop. Distance is the fill minus the stop.
wrong.The 11.21 entry; it has more room: More room to the stop means farther from it, not closer: 3.7% against 2.3%.

questions.simple: The 11.05 entry sits closer to the same stop, so its stop is tighter.

deeper.counter: Confirmation costs distance. The ORB entry waits for the range to be proven and fills at 11.21 instead of 11.05. So the same stop sits farther away: 3.7% against 2.3%. The first entry earned about 2.3R to the ORB's 1.0R. One example, not a promise that the earlier entry always wins.

reasons: one cited example row (c07) carries the numbers
the 3.7% to the stop sits above the 3.5% Kicker cap; the owner flag asks whether the cap counts the few-cents buffer
rests on the owner's Kicker ruling

questions.q: Our rulebook has no time-of-day rule; the 30 minutes on an ORB define the trigger, not a cut-off for taking it.
questions.why: True. No time-of-day rule. The 30-minute window is part of the trigger's definition; the trigger stays valid for the rest of that session.
questions.lesson_line: The clock builds the range. It does not close the trade.

questions.story: The 30-minute low is 412.06 and the break fills at 418.46.
questions.q: Where exactly is the stop?
choices: A few cents under 412.06
Exactly 412.06
A flat 3% under the fill
Under the prior day's low
questions.why: A few cents under 412.06, not exactly on it. FFIV's stop was 412.01, 1.54% under the fill: the day's low at the fill, with a little room for a tick.
questions.lesson_line: Under the low, not on it. A stop on the exact low gets ticked.

wrong.Exactly 412.06: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
wrong.A flat 3% under the fill: A percent is not a level. 3% is where the honest stop usually lands, not where it is set.
wrong.Under the prior day's low: Too far on a first break. The range low is the honest level.

questions.story: Two ranges at 10:00. In one, the high was touched twice and price sat just under it. In the other, no high repeats and the bars swing both ways.
questions.q: Which grades higher?
choices: The first; its high is well defined
The second; it has more room to run
Equal; any high is as good as another
Neither; skip both of the ranges
questions.answer: The first; its high is well defined
questions.why: The first range. A grade cue: the range high is well defined, tested more than once, or a tight consolidation sits just under it. Bysshe: if the OR is sloppy, with no well-defined support or resistance, don't waste your time watching it.
questions.lesson_line: A range you can draw is a range you can trade. Sloppy means no level.

wrong.The second; it has more room to run: No clear high gives no clear level to buy. Bysshe: with no well-defined support or resistance, don't waste your time watching it.
wrong.Equal; any high is as good as another: The grade cue is a well-defined high, tested more than once. The second range has none.
wrong.Neither; skip both of the ranges: The first range has a clear, tested high, a level worth watching. Bysshe's skip is for the sloppy range only.

questions.simple: The first range grades higher, because its high is a clear level to buy and the other has no clear level.

deeper.trap: Sloppy can look like energy, with bars all over the place. But a trigger needs a level and a stop needs a low. Bysshe: if there isn't any well-defined support or resistance, don't waste your time watching it. OVV is the clean case: a tight hold just under the range high, then a trigger at 10:30.

reasons: the cue is the card's proposal and E50 says grading is discretionary

questions.story: FFIV, 2026-09-15: a leader, RS 81, above its 50 and 200-day, flat open on 2.67x volume. The first 30-minute candle runs 412.06 to 418.45.
questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, first trim.
choices: Market 418.46; stop 412.01; third at 3R
Market 418.46; stop 412.06; flat at 3R
Limit 418.46; stop 412.01; third at 2R
Market 418.46; stop 412.06; third at 2R
questions.why: Market at 418.46, stop 412.01, a third at 3R. Buy at market as it trades a cent through the 418.45 range high. Put the stop a few cents under the day's low, and take the first third at 3R. FFIV reached 3R in two sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, trim, trail. Write the rule before the open; the range fills in the numbers at 10:00.

wrong.Market 418.46; stop 412.06; flat at 3R: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not on it. And the hard rule is a third at 3R, not all of it.
wrong.Limit 418.46; stop 412.01; third at 2R: Entries are market orders. And 2R is where breakeven may start, not a trim. The hard rule is a third at 3R.
wrong.Market 418.46; stop 412.06; third at 2R: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it. And 2R is a breakeven level, not the first trim.

questions.simple: Buy at market through the high, put the stop a few cents under the low, and sell a third at 3R.

deeper.example: FFIV, 2026-09-15: the rule written before the open gave, at 10:00, a buy at 418.46 and a stop of 412.01. That is a few cents under the 412.06 low and 1.54% under the fill. It broke the range on the first bar after 10:00 and reached 3R in two sessions.

reasons: rests on rulebook E57, F62 and B19
a buy-stop (D-038) would not change this key
numbers come from one dossier scan row

questions.story: You bought at 60.92 with the stop at 59.51, so 2R below your entry is 58.10. Next week it gaps open at 58.90 and the first 30-minute low prints 57.20.
questions.q: What does the gap rule say?
choices: Get out; the loss is past 2R
The 57.20 low is the new stop
Sell at the open price, 58.90
Hold; wait and see the close
questions.answer: Get out; the loss is past 2R
questions.why: Get out. After a gap against the stop, the first 30-minute low becomes the new stop. There is a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you leave. One R is 60.92 minus 59.51, so 2R below the entry is 58.10. The first 30-minute low of 57.20 is under it.
questions.lesson_line: The gap rule gives the first 30 minutes, not a blank cheque. Past 2R, you are out.

wrong.Hold; wait and see the close: The stop is the exit. There is no rule that waits for a close after a gap through it.
wrong.The 57.20 low is the new stop: The 30-minute low becomes the stop only inside the 2R ceiling. This one is past it.
wrong.Sell at the open price, 58.90: The rule gives the first 30 minutes. The open is not the decision; the 30-minute low is.

questions.simple: Get out, because the first 30 minutes took the loss past 2R, so the 30-minute low does not become the stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is using the new stop without checking the ceiling. The gap opened at 58.90, still above the 2R line at 58.10, so the open alone does not force an exit. But the first 30 minutes printed 57.20, under that line. The 30-minute low is the new stop only while it stays inside 2R.

reasons: rests on rulebook B20 and its 2R ceiling
a computed key (2R level)

questions.story: Same stock, same week: you were stopped out on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, one try each day. Thursday morning a new break prints.
questions.q: Buy it?
choices: No; three tries a week is the cap
Yes; a new trigger is a new trade
Yes, if you cut it to half size
No; the cap is two tries a week
questions.answer: No; three tries a week is the cap
questions.why: No. The same stock: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month. Each buy was a new trade and each one counted, so Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday used the three. A fourth on Thursday is over the line.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries a week and six a month on one stock. A fourth try in the same week is a pass.

wrong.Yes; a new trigger is a new trade: Each new trigger is a new trade, and each one counts. The cap is 3 a week.
wrong.Yes, if you cut it to half size: Size does not reset the count. Three is three.
wrong.No; the cap is two tries a week: The cap is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month, not two.

questions.simple: No, because the same stock gets at most 3 tries a week, and Monday through Wednesday used all three.

deeper.trap: 'A new trigger is a new trade' is true, and that is why the count matters. Each try had its own stop and every rule, and each one counted. Three in a week on one stock is the weekly cap; six in a month is the monthly cap.

reasons: rests on rulebook E56 and B21; a week is not defined in the rulebook

questions.story: A leader reported last night and gaps 3% this morning on heavy volume. At 10:05 it trades through its 30-minute high.
questions.q: Take the break?
choices: Yes; the window has passed
Yes, but only after 11:00
No; no buys near earnings
No; wait three sessions after
questions.why: Yes. The rule is no new buy in the 3 sessions before an earnings report. This leader reported last night, so that window has passed. An ORB on the day after the report is allowed. The 5R test is only for holding a trade through a report.
questions.lesson_line: The blackout is before the report, not after it.

wrong.Yes, but only after 11:00: We have no time-of-day rule. A trade through the high is the trigger all session.
wrong.No; no buys near earnings: Near is not the rule. Before is. The report is done.
wrong.No; wait three sessions after: The 3 sessions sit before the report, not after it.

questions.simple: Yes, take it. The earnings rule blocks new buys in the 3 sessions before a report, and this report is already out.

deeper.example: The card names TMDX, APPS and GRRR as ORBs taken on the day after a report. The blackout sits before the report: no new buy in the 3 sessions before one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)
