questions.q: Kullamagi sells a third to a half after 3 to 5 days. Our rule sells a third at 3R and a third at 5R.
questions.why: True. Kullamagi: sell a third to a half after 3 to 5 days, then move the stop to breakeven. Ours sells by R: a third at 3R, another at 5R, then the trail.
questions.lesson_line: His clock, our ladder. Same stop, different exit.

questions.story: You bought the ORB at the size your plan set. It runs through the next daily level an hour later and keeps going.
questions.q: Add through the level?
choices: No; full size at one price, no adds
Yes; strength deserves a bigger stake
Yes, a third more with the same stop
No; take it all off at that level
questions.answer: No; full size at one price, no adds
questions.why: No. The full size goes in at one price with one stop; no adding. The next level is not a second entry. Strength is handled by the thirds at 3R and 5R and by the trail.
questions.lesson_line: One fill, one stop, no adds. Strength is paid by the trims and the trail.

wrong.Yes, a third more with the same stop: The rule is one price, one stop and no adding, so a third more breaks it.
wrong.Yes; strength deserves a bigger stake: Strength is paid by the thirds and the trail, not by a bigger position. The rule is full size at one price.
wrong.No; take it all off at that level: The ladder sells a third at 3R, another at 5R, and trails the rest. It does not sell everything at a level.

questions.simple: No, because we buy full size at one price with one stop and never add, however strong the move runs.

deeper.trap: Adding feels like trusting a winner. But the rulebook sizes the whole trade at the fill, from the account, the risk percent and the distance to the stop. The full size goes in at one price with one stop. The next daily level is not a second entry. Strength is paid by the thirds at 3R and 5R and by the trail.

reasons: rests on rulebook A5 (no adding)

questions.story: Two 10:00 breaks. One stays above the range high for 20 minutes. The other goes above it, drops back inside after 3 minutes, then goes above it again.
questions.q: Which grades higher?
choices: The first, the break that held
The second; it broke out twice
Equal; both made the trigger
Neither; only a close counts
questions.answer: The first, the break that held
questions.why: The first break, the one that held 20 minutes. A quick, clean break that holds above the range high for about 15 minutes is a grade cue. That is Bysshe's half-the-range-time rule, half of a 30-minute range. A break that falls back inside has not held.
questions.lesson_line: A good break holds above the range high. Fifteen minutes is the rule of thumb.

wrong.The second; it broke out twice: A break that falls back inside the range has not held. Holding is the cue, not breaking twice.
wrong.Equal; both made the trigger: Both triggered. Only one held, and holding is the grade cue.
wrong.Neither; only a close counts: The trigger is the trade through the high, not a close. Both breaks triggered.

questions.simple: The 20-minute hold grades higher, because a good break holds above the range high for about 15 minutes.

deeper.trap: The 3-minute break is a trigger, since the first trade through the high is. The grade asks whether it held. Bysshe's test: trade above the range for half the range's length, about 15 minutes on a 30-minute range. A break that falls back inside after 3 minutes fails that test. A big-volume reversal back into the range is the classic failure shape.

reasons: the cue is the card's proposal and E50 says grading is discretionary
Bysshe's quote sits in a PDF the quote script cannot match, read by hand

questions.story: Two ORB longs in our window were stopped out the same day. Neither ever got past +0.26R, and each stop sat about 2% under the fill.
questions.q: What kept each loss at 1R?
choices: The stop under the day's low
Selling at the first reversal
A wider stop, to give it room
The 4% limit on chasing the fill
questions.answer: The stop under the day's low
questions.why: The stop under the day's low. Whatever the break was missing, the stop is what kept each loss at 1R. It sits a few cents under the day's low, it only moves up, and it is a real order with the broker. A loss at that stop is the plan working.
questions.lesson_line: You will take this loss again. The stop is why it stays small.

wrong.Selling at the first reversal: The reversal is a warning. The stop was the exit, and it did the work.
wrong.A wider stop, to give it room: The stop only moves up, never down or wider.
wrong.The 4% limit on chasing the fill: The 4% line limits how far above the buy point you may buy. It does not size the loss.

questions.simple: The stop kept each loss at 1R. A loss at the planned stop is the plan working.

deeper.trap: A 1R loss is the plan working, but the cause still matters. Across the four losses we read, the missing piece was the parent setup, the direction of the open or the calendar. Check those before the buy, not after the stop.
